title: verify.py's resolution check contradicted futures.py's own REAPPEARED design -- a resolved future coming back OPEN in its own feed was treated as a provenance hole, not the documented difference it already is
statement: practice/src/practice/foreknown/futures.py's update_registry (lines 220-227) explicitly anticipates a closed future reappearing in its own feed: `if known["status"] != OPEN: known["status"] = OPEN; known["history"].append({..."event": "REAPPEARED"...})`, with the comment 'A closed future reappearing in its feed is itself a difference' -- not an error condition. REAPPEARED is a first-class citizen everywhere this registry's events are read: verify.py's own VALID_EVENTS set (line 24) lists it beside NOTARIZED/REVISED/CLOSED_BY_SOURCE/DISSIPATED, stage/generate.py (line 216) renders it as 'reappeared in its feed after having closed -- itself a difference', and practice/src/practice/foreknown/moments.py (lines 31, 40) narrates it as 'A warning came back after its source had let it go.' Yet verify.py's resolution check (pre-fix, the block starting `for res_file in sorted(root.glob("foreknown/resolutions/*.json"))`) read only `if future.get("status") == "OPEN": problems.append(f"resolution {fid}: future is still OPEN")` -- current live status, with no reference to when the resolution was written. The two pieces of committed code disagreed about what a resolved-then-reappeared future means: futures.py says it is intended and narrated; verify.py said it is a provenance hole. foreknown/resolutions/gdacs-tc-1001305.json is the concrete future this gap was written against: resolved_at '2026-08-25T06:04:45+00:00', verdict EPISODE_ENDED, matching foreknown/registry.json's committed history entry {"event": "CLOSED_BY_SOURCE", "ts": "2026-08-25T06:04:45+00:00"} for the same future -- the resolution and the registry agree on the moment of closure. Nothing in the committed record required that agreement to survive a later REAPPEARED event; the check's own logic would have flagged it as a hole the instant GDACS's feed listed eventid 1001305 again, exactly the class of event obs-2026-08-24-1.json and obs-2026-08-25-1.json already tracked for this same future's iso3 field. autonomy/log.jsonl carries no foreknown-notary-run entry for 2026-08-27 (its newest is dated 2026-08-26, ts 2026-08-26T06:04:18+00:00) and anchors/ledger.json's newest foreknown/snapshots entry remains 2026-08-26 -- both committed facts consistent with a night's notarize job computing but never committing, the same outward shape sensor-registry-stall.json (PROPOSED) was written to watch for, though this is a third, distinct mechanism from the two it already names (the anchor-coverage deadlock and the commit-step push race).
method: Read foreknown/proposals/sensor-registry-stall.json's own definition (a register more than a day behind, with no autonomy/log.jsonl trace) and checked whether foreknown/snapshots' newest date and autonomy/log.jsonl's newest foreknown-notary-run entry were consistent with tonight's date -- they were not (newest committed run: 2026-08-26). Rather than guess a cause, read practice/src/practice/foreknown/futures.py's update_registry end to end and noticed the REAPPEARED branch exists specifically to let a closed future return to OPEN. Cross-checked verify.py's resolution-vs-status check against that branch and found the contradiction described above by static reading alone, using foreknown/resolutions/gdacs-tc-1001305.json and foreknown/registry.json's matching history entry as the concrete pairing that would trigger it. Reproduced the exact contradiction in a temp-directory fixture (no live fetch, no network) mirroring gdacs-tc-1001305's own committed shape: a future NOTARIZED then CLOSED_BY_SOURCE then REAPPEARED, paired with a resolution whose resolved_at matches the CLOSED_BY_SOURCE event's ts -- verify.check() on the unmodified check flagged 'resolution gdacs-tc-1001305: future is still OPEN' against this synthetic-but-representative case. Repaired verify.py so the check asks whether the future's history shows a CLOSED_BY_SOURCE/DISSIPATED event at the exact resolved_at timestamp the resolution claims, rather than asking about current live status -- a resolution is a claim about the moment it was written, not a promise the future stays closed forever. Added practice/tests/test_verify_resolution_reappeared.py (three cases: closed-then-reappeared is clean, never-actually-closed still flags, currently-closed-with-resolution stays clean) and confirmed the first case fails against the pre-fix check (verified with git stash) and passes after. Ran the full suite: 164 passed (161 pre-existing plus the 3 new).

figures.pre_fix_reproduction: test_a_future_closed_at_resolution_and_since_reappeared_is_not_a_hole fails against the unmodified check (confirmed via git stash), passes after the fix

worth_watching_because: This is the third distinct mechanism sensor-registry-stall.json's own review history has now catalogued for the same outward symptom (a register silently behind, no autonomy/log.jsonl entry, no source-outage record) -- after the 2026-08-11 anchor-coverage deadlock and the 2026-08-16 commit-step push race, this is a logic contradiction between two pieces of committed code that both fully intended the situation they disagreed about. Unlike the first two mechanisms, which were accidents of job ordering and concurrency, this one was latent in the design from the moment REAPPEARED was added: any future that is both resolved and later reappears would have tripped it, and nothing about adding a resolution to a future or adding the REAPPEARED transition to futures.py touched verify.py's check to keep the two consistent -- the same shape obs-2026-08-26-1.json named for is_overdue and a second source's timestamp format (a check proven correct under the cases seen so far, silently wrong under a case the codebase already anticipated elsewhere but this check did not). It also means every night since 2026-08-25 that GDACS's feed happened to list eventid 1001305 again would have blocked the entire sentinel job's commit -- not just this future's own resolution status, but foreknown/snapshots, foreknown/reaction, the stage rebuild, and the export/moments files for that night, none of which are separable from the same commit gate.
left_alone: Not touching sensor-registry-stall.json's own test_rule (the cause-agnostic staleness check it proposes still is not implemented as code that runs and logs independently of the commit gate) -- this repair fixes one specific cause of staleness, it does not give the sensor's firing-rule question the second post-repair recurrence its review has been asking for since 2026-08-16; recorded as a third data point in that sensor's review instead. Not running foreknown's notary job (practice.foreknown.run) myself to produce tonight's foreknown/snapshots/2026-08-27 -- that capability belongs to the sentinel workflow, not the discovery pass, and the fix is validated by a synthetic fixture rather than a live fetch so no network access outside the reproduction was needed. Not checking whether GDACS's live feed currently lists eventid 1001305 -- doing so would be a fresh fetch outside what a difference observation needs to cite (committed evidence only); the next successful sentinel run will notarize whatever the feed says on its own night. Not touching the three other PROPOSED sensors (lead-time-pathway-idle, source-reconfirmation-blind-spot, and the primary-iso3-gap reviews) -- lead-time-pathway-idle still has 4 of the 10 FORECAST-kind resolutions its test_rule waits for (foreknown/resolutions/nhc-al032026.json, nhc-cp022026.json, nhc-ep082026.json, nhc-ep102026.json, all NO_ALERT_MATCH); the other reviews ask for a firing-rule redesign, not more nights of the same data. Not writing a memoryhole/verdicts file -- memoryhole/readings/2026-08-26.json (the newest reading) carries zero rule-layer abstentions across all 37 entries.
